title: Your short video may be losing viewers before the point arrives
markdown:
# Your short video may be losing viewers before the point arrives

At 8:07, you post a 24-second clip you spent an hour editing. The first frame is your logo. Then comes a greeting, then a sentence that starts with "So today I want to talk about..." By the time the useful part appears, the viewer has already flicked to the next video.

That is a painful problem because it can make a good idea look like a bad one. The fix is rarely a louder edit or a more dramatic voice. It is deciding what a stranger needs to see or hear before they give you another second.

TikTok's own small-business guide puts it plainly: show the product in action, ask a relatable question, make a bold statement, or reveal a transformation early. It also advises creators to skip long intros and logo animations. [Its Creative Center guidance](https://ads.tiktok.com/business/en/guides/video-advertising-guide?redirected=1) treats the first three seconds as the place to earn attention, not to introduce yourself.

## A hook is a promise you can keep

The word "hook" has been damaged by a lot of bad advice. It can suggest bait: say something outrageous, hide the answer, make the viewer wait. That approach may buy a few seconds, but it also trains people not to trust you.

A usable hook makes a small, specific promise and then pays it off quickly. If the video is about a cheaper way to light a desk, open with the dim desk and the change in light. If it is about a bookkeeping mistake, show the line item that caused the surprise. If it is about baking, show the cracked first batch before you explain what changed.

The opening does not need to explain the whole video. It needs to make the next beat feel worth watching.

TikTok's Creative Center makes a related point: the hook should connect to the key message that follows. A striking opening that belongs to a different video creates a clean swipe the moment the viewer realizes the switch.

## Find the thing the viewer recognizes before they recognize you

Most weak openings begin with the maker's context. "I have been testing..." "I wanted to share..." "A lot of people asked..." The viewer has no reason to care about any of that yet.

Start instead with a recognizable moment in the viewer's day. For a freelancer: "If every client note turns into a different to-do list, this is the line you are missing." For a home cook: "This is why your garlic burns before the onions soften." For a fitness coach: "If your knees cave in on the last two reps, do not start by blaming your shoes."

Each opening gives the right person a quick reason to stop. It also gives everyone else permission to move on, which is useful. A hook aimed at everyone usually lands as wallpaper.

Write the viewer's moment in one sentence before writing any hook. Be concrete about the frustration, the object in frame, and the result they want. "Creators need better hooks" is too broad. "A creator watches people leave before the demonstration begins" gives you something to work with.

## Draft several openings, then reject the clever ones

One good idea can produce different hook shapes. Try a few against the same promise:

- Show the before-and-after first.
- Name a mistake the viewer can see in their own work.
- Ask a question whose answer changes a decision they are making today.
- State the result, then immediately show the condition that made it possible.
- Begin in the middle of the action, with the evidence already on screen.

Do not choose the line that sounds most impressive on a notes app. Choose the one that can be understood with the sound off, fits the first shot, and leads naturally into the actual point. TikTok also recommends captions for clarity and a benefit-focused call to action; that is a useful reminder that a spoken line is only one part of the opening.

Read each candidate aloud at normal speed. If it takes four seconds before the viewer knows what it is about, cut it. If the first visual and the first sentence make separate promises, rewrite one of them. If the payoff is not in the video, throw the hook away.

## Match the opening to the evidence you have

A claim-based hook needs proof soon after it. "I cut my edit time in half" invites a number, a comparison, or a clear demonstration. A visual hook needs a visible change. A question needs an answer that is more useful than "it depends."

This is where many videos get vague. The opening says "Stop doing this," then the rest of the clip offers general encouragement. Instead, give the viewer a move they can try in the next take: put the finished result in frame first, replace an introduction with the problem, or put the key noun in the first caption.

You do not need a different personality for every video. You need a repeatable way to test the first beat while keeping the promise honest.

## Turn a blank first line into options

When you are staring at an empty script, use a hook-writing session to generate angles from the real video rather than borrowing somebody else's catchphrase. Describe the viewer, the moment they are in, what changes by the end, and what proof you can show. Then keep only the lines that belong to the footage you can make.

[Hook Lab can help you draft and pressure-test those opening options.](https://capafy.ai/agent/8123079349?ct=hooklab_blog)

The goal is not to trick somebody into watching. It is to let the right viewer recognize, in the first few seconds, that this video has an answer for the problem they already have.
